title: Seattle Ecommerce Website Brief: Catalogue, Migration & Launch Checklist
meta_title: Seattle Ecommerce Website Brief & Launch Checklist
meta_desc: Prepare a Seattle ecommerce project brief covering products, migration, checkout, integrations and launch checks. Compare quotes with a practical scope worksheet.
excerpt: Prepare a Seattle ecommerce project brief covering products, migration, checkout, integrations and launch checks. Compare quotes with a practical scope worksheet.
content:
Quick Answer

A useful ecommerce brief records products, customer journeys, integrations, migration needs and launch checks. Send a representative product sample and your current store URL before asking for a fixed quote. This gives the developer enough context to separate a straightforward store build from a complex operational project.

Start with the Store You Need to Operate

A Seattle retailer asking for a new ecommerce website may actually need several different things: a cleaner product catalogue, a better mobile buying journey, fewer manual order tasks, or a migration from an ageing platform. “Build a Shopify store” does not explain which problem comes first. Without that context, two quotes can look similar while covering very different work.

This brief is a practical worksheet for a store owner, not a price list or a promise of higher revenue. Use it when preparing an enquiry for Seattle ecommerce development. It also helps an existing store team decide whether a redesign, platform migration or smaller improvement project is the right next step.

Write one primary goal in plain language. For example: customers should find the right replacement part without calling; staff should stop re-entering orders into the fulfilment system; or the current product pages should explain sizes and delivery before checkout. Each goal suggests different discovery questions and acceptance checks.

1. Inventory Products, Variants and Content

Record how many products you actively sell, how many variants each product has and which attributes customers use to choose. A catalogue with twenty products and several sizes is different from a parts catalogue with compatibility rules, technical specifications and thousands of variants. Product count alone does not explain that difference.

Give your developer a sample containing one simple product, one product with several options and one difficult edge case. Include names, SKUs, images, prices, stock status, weights, descriptions and any custom fields. A sample reveals missing information before a migration estimate depends on data that has never been inspected.

Identify who owns product copy and image cleanup. If the source files contain duplicate SKUs, unclear option names or inconsistent units, agree whether your team or the developer will fix them. Put that responsibility in the scope, together with how corrected data will be approved.

Brief itemExample decisionAcceptance evidence
Products and optionsWhich variants need separate stock or images?An agreed sample product behaves correctly
Navigation and filtersHow will customers narrow the catalogue?Priority products are reachable on mobile
Stock and fulfilmentWhere is the authoritative inventory held?A test order follows the agreed operational path
Content ownershipWho supplies descriptions, images and policies?Required content is approved before launch

2. Describe the Customer Journey Before Selecting a Platform

List the pages and steps a buyer needs: collection browsing, search results, product information, cart, checkout and confirmation. If you sell to both consumers and trade buyers, identify which differences genuinely matter. Separate prices, approval workflows, minimum quantities or account rules can materially change the build.

Shopify, WooCommerce and custom development should be compared against those requirements rather than chosen because a competitor uses one. Document the features that must be built, those a maintained app or extension can support, and those that can wait. Include ownership and maintenance responsibilities in the comparison.

A store with a good checkout may still need clearer product details. A site with useful content may instead have a broken shipping rule. Ask the team to explain which parts need changing and what evidence supports the recommendation. A narrowly scoped improvement can be more useful than replacing an entire platform without a clear operational reason.

3. Specify Payments, Shipping and Integrations

Create a list of payment providers, shipping destinations, pickup options, fulfilment tools and required business-system connections. Name the integration and the task it should perform. “CRM integration” might mean passing an enquiry into a pipeline, syncing customer records, or automating an order workflow; those are different scopes.

Confirm who can provide access and approve business settings. Payment-provider availability, account approval and recurring fees should be checked separately from the development quote. Tax configuration should follow the business requirements confirmed by the appropriate adviser; a website brief is not tax advice.

For each integration, agree a success condition and a failure condition. What happens if inventory cannot sync, a payment is declined, or a fulfilment request is delayed? Decide what staff should see, whether a retry is appropriate and who investigates. This is also where you identify paid app subscriptions and ongoing vendor costs.

4. Define What Migration Actually Includes

A migration should name each data type instead of treating “move the store” as a single task. Products, pages, customers, historical orders, reviews and store credits may require different methods. Specify what is required, what the destination supports and how the result will be checked.

Shopify’s migration guide distinguishes transfer methods for different kinds of store data and includes checks after import. For your project, request a sample migration before agreeing to move the entire catalogue. Review the sample with the person who operates the store.

The WooCommerce product CSV documentation explains its product import and export workflow. Do not assume a product CSV also represents every customer, historical order or extension-specific field. List the required data types and confirm a supported method for each one.

Inventory existing URLs as a separate workstream. Where a page address changes, map it to the most relevant new destination and check the redirect. Google’s site-move guidance covers URL mapping, redirects and monitoring. Redirecting every old product to the homepage is not a useful substitute for that map.

5. Use a Launch Acceptance Checklist

Ask for a written acceptance checklist that you can understand and review. A successful launch is more than a homepage loading on the developer’s laptop. Select representative products, variants and shipping scenarios, then agree which devices and account states will be checked.

A practical checklist can include a successful test order, a declined payment, a discount, a shipping boundary, a pickup order where offered, and the correct confirmation message. Verify that the order appears in the expected system and that staff can complete their part of the workflow. Use provider-approved test modes when available.

Also review customer support information, broken links, image behaviour and keyboard access on agreed templates. Record analytics events that matter to the business, such as product views, checkout starts and confirmed purchases. A button click and a completed paid order should not be counted as the same outcome.

6. Compare Quotes with a Scope Worksheet

Compare deliverables rather than the headline price. Ask each proposal to name included templates, product handling, migration effort, integrations, review rounds, launch support and exclusions. Two estimates are not comparable when one assumes ready-to-use content and the other includes extensive catalogue cleanup.

Separate initial implementation from recurring costs. Hosting, platform plans, paid themes, apps, transaction-related charges and maintenance should have a named owner and a current price source. Do not use an old blog estimate as the final budget for a provider subscription.

A change process is useful too. If the product sample reveals a new workflow, who approves the extra work and its effect on the launch date? Decide how changes are documented before the project begins. That makes the budget easier to manage without pretending that every requirement is already known.

Quote lineQuestion to ask
Design and templatesWhich distinct layouts and review rounds are included?
Catalogue and migrationWhich records move, and who fixes source data?
IntegrationsWhich connections, access dependencies and tests are included?
Launch and handoverWho approves launch, receives access and maintains the store?
Recurring costsWhich subscriptions and support arrangements are separate?

7. Send a Brief That Makes the First Conversation Useful

Your first enquiry can be short: current store URL, primary goal, product and variant counts, preferred platform if any, required integrations, migration needs and desired launch window. Attach or describe a representative product sample. If something is undecided, say so rather than filling the brief with guesses.

For remote collaboration, agree review windows in Pacific Time and assign one person to consolidate feedback. Chulbul Design is based in Gurugram, India and serves Seattle remotely. We can review the requirements and propose a scope without claiming a Seattle office or a local client result.

Ready to prepare a project estimate? Visit our Seattle ecommerce project enquiry form. For a service-led company website rather than an online store, compare the broader Seattle web design services.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does a Seattle ecommerce website cost?

The cost depends on catalogue complexity, design, integrations, migration and testing. Request a written quote based on a sample catalogue and defined deliverables. The $799 starter website offer is a limited company-website scope, not a complete ecommerce-store price.

Can I request a quote before choosing Shopify or WooCommerce?

Yes. Explain the customer journey, catalogue and operational needs first. The platform comparison can be part of discovery, with maintenance responsibilities and recurring costs documented.

Should every old page move to the new store?

Inventory the existing content and agree which pages remain useful. Where important URLs change, specify relevant destinations and test the redirects. Avoid deleting useful content simply because the design is changing.

What should I send with my first enquiry?

Send the store URL, main problem, approximate product and variant counts, key integrations and launch window. A small sample of product data helps the team identify migration and catalogue issues early.

title: Seattle Contractor Website Lead Audit: Forms, Delivery & Follow-Up
meta_title: Seattle Contractor Website Lead Audit Checklist
meta_desc: Audit contractor website leads: relevant visits, mobile contact actions, forms, saved enquiries, notifications and follow-up. Practical checklist for Seattle teams.
excerpt: Audit contractor website leads: relevant visits, mobile contact actions, forms, saved enquiries, notifications and follow-up. Practical checklist for Seattle teams.
content:
Quick Answer

Audit the whole lead journey: relevant visits, service information, contact actions, form validation, database storage, notifications and follow-up. Test each stage separately. A quiet inbox does not by itself prove that the website is receiving no enquiries.

Start by Finding Where the Enquiry Journey Stops

A contractor website can stop producing useful enquiries for different reasons. Fewer homeowners may be reaching the site. The page may describe the wrong services. The quote form might ask for too much information. A saved enquiry might not reach the person responsible for responding. These problems need different fixes.

This guide gives Seattle contractors and home-service businesses a practical audit sequence. Use it before commissioning a full redesign or increasing advertising spend. It is also a useful project brief for contractor web design in Seattle, because it connects each website change to a customer task and an operational check.

Begin with one priority service and one page. A focused inspection is easier to act on than a long list of general improvements. Write down what a good enquiry looks like: the right job type, a genuine service area, enough contact information and a next step your team can handle.

1. Compare Visits Before Judging the Form

Separate visibility, visits and enquiries. Search impressions show that a result appeared; clicks show that someone selected it. A site visit still does not prove that the visitor wanted the service you sell. Review the search queries, landing pages and channels associated with the work you actually want.

Compare similar periods and note changes in campaigns, business availability and measurement setup. If analytics was recently installed, it cannot reconstruct a missing history. If advertising was paused, a lower enquiry count may reflect fewer visits rather than a broken form. Treat small samples cautiously.

Record a baseline for the chosen page: visits, contact clicks, form starts, submission attempts, confirmed saved enquiries and qualified jobs. Define the terms before comparing counts. A submission attempt that fails validation should not be reported as a successfully received lead.

StageWhat to inspectLikely next check
Relevant visitsChannels, queries and landing pagesDoes the audience match the service?
Contact intentPhone, email and quote actionsAre the actions clear on mobile?
SubmissionValidation errors and response stateCan a visitor complete the form?
DeliveryStored records and notificationsDid the right team receive the enquiry?
Follow-upResponse ownership and lead qualityWas the visitor contacted appropriately?

2. Make the Service Clear in the First Screen

A homeowner should quickly understand the trade, the kind of work offered and how to request an estimate. A heading full of slogans can hide those answers. Use a concise service heading and a short explanation of the job types your business actually accepts.

Describe real coverage rather than implying a crew or office in every nearby place. Seattle, Bellevue and other areas should appear only when the business genuinely serves them. If travel limits, scheduling constraints or project minimums affect suitability, explain them where customers make their decision.

Make the next action visible. A short quote request, a call link or a booking route should fit how the team responds. If calls are not staffed throughout the day, do not promise instant service. The website should set an accurate expectation and offer an alternative when appropriate.

3. Give Visitors Proof Relevant to the Job

Use genuine project photographs and explain the work shown. A useful caption identifies the service and practical scope without revealing private customer information. Before-and-after images should be accurate, authorised and easy to view on a phone. Decorative stock photography is not evidence that the contractor completed a project.

Connect proof to the relevant service page. A visitor considering a roof repair should not have to inspect an unrelated gallery to understand your experience. Explain what was assessed, what work was performed and what the business can verify, rather than adding unsupported revenue or satisfaction claims.

Reviews, licences, insurance details and memberships should be checked by the business before publication. Use accurate attribution and appropriate source links for reviews. This audit is about presenting verified information clearly; it is not a reason to invent credentials or promise results that a website cannot guarantee.

4. Reduce the First Form to Useful Contact Information

For an initial conversation, ask for the information the team genuinely needs to respond. Name and one reliable contact method may be enough. A short job description or service choice can help route the enquiry, but a long questionnaire can be saved for follow-up when it is not essential to the first step.

Allow email or phone if your operation can support both. Requiring a telephone number from every visitor may exclude people who prefer a written estimate discussion. If a field is optional, label it clearly. If you need a postcode or property type to screen work, explain why rather than asking without context.

The W3C forms tutorial covers labels, instructions, validation and feedback. Use those principles to check that visitors understand the fields and can recover from an error. A placeholder that disappears while typing should not be the only label.

On mobile, inspect the field keyboard, button size and visible error message. Ask someone unfamiliar with the site to request an estimate without instructions. Observe where they hesitate, but do not infer a universal conversion-rate uplift from one informal test.

5. Check the Form Beyond the Success Message

A success message is only one part of the delivery chain. Confirm that a valid enquiry produces a stored record, that the record contains the intended service and page attribution, and that the team can find it. Then verify the notification route separately.

Use a clearly identified test and agree who will receive any notification before sending it. Check email-only and phone-only submissions where supported, an invalid address, missing required details and a network or server error. A failed request should preserve the visitor’s information so they can correct or retry it.

A database record does not guarantee email inbox delivery. A mail server accepting a message also does not prove that the recipient saw it. Compare the stored record, server notification result and recipient inbox instead of treating them as a single signal. Check spam handling and the destination address with the person responsible for leads.

Keep tests distinct from genuine enquiries in reports. Avoid placing customer names, phone numbers or email addresses into analytics event labels. Lead attribution usually needs the page, service and channel; personal contact information belongs in the appropriate business system.

6. Test Calls, Email and WhatsApp Routes

A call button should open the right number on a phone. An email link should address the correct inbox. A WhatsApp link should use the intended destination and an accurate initial message. Check these actions on the actual page rather than assuming a working footer means every service CTA is correct.

International format matters when a team serves customers remotely. Do not silently add an Indian country code to a Seattle visitor’s phone number. Preserve the supplied number and confirm unclear country codes before using it for follow-up.

Give the visitor a clear fallback when a form fails. An accessible email or WhatsApp route can help them continue the conversation. It is still important to fix the original failure and record submission outcomes; a fallback should not hide a broken enquiry system.

7. Assign Follow-Up Ownership

Agree who reads the enquiry inbox, who checks the stored leads and who responds when the main person is unavailable. A shared mailbox without a clear owner can create unanswered requests even when the website works correctly.

Track practical outcomes: contacted, suitable job, outside service area, duplicate, spam or not proceeding. Define these categories consistently and keep contact details out of general analytics reports. Over time, the categories can show whether the page attracts unsuitable work or whether response handling needs attention.

Publish a response expectation your business can meet. If reviews or project meetings take place in Pacific Time while the website team is elsewhere, make the schedule clear. Chulbul Design delivers Seattle website projects remotely from Gurugram, India; that delivery arrangement does not imply local contractor crews or emergency availability.

8. Prioritise Repairs Before a Full Redesign

Fix a broken delivery route before polishing a gallery. Fix misleading service information before buying more traffic to that page. Move a buried contact action into a useful position before adding several new sections that make the page longer. Priorities should follow the observed failure, not a standard redesign checklist.

Create a short repair log with the issue, affected page, owner, acceptance check and completion date. After each change, repeat the relevant test and compare like-for-like outcomes over a useful period. Seasonal demand and small samples can make immediate results noisy.

For a wider company website, review our Seattle small business web design service. For a site whose editing, plugin or maintenance problems require a WordPress specialist, see our Seattle WordPress development page.

If you need help defining the repairs, send your current website, priority trade, genuine service areas and the point where enquiries seem to stop through the contractor website project enquiry form. We can discuss the scope without guaranteeing a ranking or a particular number of leads.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a new contractor website guarantee more leads?

No. Lead volume depends on relevant traffic, demand, competition, service fit, trust, contact usability and follow-up. A redesign should address observed problems and be measured against clear outcomes.

Should a quote form require a phone number?

Only if phone contact is genuinely necessary for your workflow. If your team can respond by email, allowing either email or phone can support more visitor preferences. Validate whichever contact method is supplied.

Why can an enquiry be saved but missing from email?

Storage and email notification are separate steps. The notification might fail, reach the wrong address or be filtered. Check the stored lead, notification result and recipient inbox independently.

What should I check first when leads drop?

Compare relevant visits and confirmed enquiry records for similar periods, then test the contact journey. Identify whether the break is traffic, page relevance, submission, delivery or response handling before choosing a repair.
